# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Mute, Blind, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: DEAF

You see the bomb: every colour on it, every marking printed on it, every reading it
gives. You hear nothing. You hold no manual, and you cannot touch the bomb.

## Your channels

When you speak, Mute and Blind receive it.
When you gesture, Mute receives it.
You never receive speech.

## Your reach

You cannot act. What this bomb can be made to do is for the one who can reach it to
find under their own hands.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

TURN 1
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [0]
LIGHT [green]
BUTTON [large] [PUSH TO DEFUSE]
WIRES 1:[red] 2:[green] 3:[yellow]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👋 🤳 ☝ ✋]
Blind gestures to Deaf: [👋 🤝]

I am Deaf. I see the bomb clearly: a green light, a large button labeled "PUSH TO DEFUSE", and three wires (red, green, yellow).

I have received gestures from both Mute and Blind.
Mute's gesture sequence is [👋 🤳 ☝ ✋].
Blind's gesture sequence is [👋 🤝].

Since I cannot hear speech, I must rely on visual cues. However, I also cannot touch the bomb or read the manual. My role is to provide visual information to those who can act or interpret rules.

The most critical piece of information for Blind (who acts) and Mute (who knows the rules) is what I see. Since they are already looking at me (presumably, as we are in a room together), I need to communicate the state of the bomb.

However, the prompt implies that communication happens via `speak` (for audio) and `gesture` (for visual).
- If I speak, Mute and Blind receive it. But wait, the rules say "Whoever can hear receives your words". Blind can hear. Mute can hear? The table says Mute "Cannot Speak". It doesn't explicitly say Mute cannot hear, but usually "Mute" implies inability to speak, not hear. Let's re-read carefully.
  - Deaf: Cannot Hear. Can See.
  - Mute: Cannot Speak. Can Read Manual. Can Hear? The table says "Cannot: Speak, or touch the bomb". It does *not* say "Cannot Hear". So Mute likely hears.
  - Blind: Cannot See. Can Reach. Can Hear? The table says "Cannot: See a colour...". It does *not* say "Cannot Hear". So Blind likely hears.

So, if I speak, both Mute and Blind will hear my words. This is the most efficient way to convey complex data like colors and labels, provided I don't use gesture symbols in the text (which would be lost on them if they couldn't see, but they *can* hear the words describing them if I describe them verbally). Wait, the rule says: "Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that gesture while you talk."
If I type "The wire is red", Mute and Blind hear "The wire is red". They do not see anything unless I gesture.
If I type "The wire is 🔴", Mute and Blind hear "The wire is [blank]" because they cannot see the emoji/gesture symbol.

Therefore, I should **speak** to convey the visual details using words, not emojis.

What about gestures?
Gestures are seen by whoever can see. Only I (Deaf) can see? No, the table says:
- Deaf: Can See.
- Mute: Can Read Manual. Can See? The table doesn't list "Cannot See" for Mute. It lists "Cannot Speak". Usually, Mute people can see.
- Blind: Cannot See.

Let's check the constraints again.
"You each hold a different piece... Deaf sees... Mute reads... Blind reaches."
It doesn't explicitly state Mute's vision status, but typically in these puzzles:
- Deaf: Sees everything, hears nothing.
- Mute: Hears everything, speaks nothing. Does he see? If he sees, he sees what Deaf sees. If he doesn't see, he relies on Deaf's gestures? But Deaf gestures go to Mute. If Mute can't see, gestures are useless.
- Blind: Hears everything, sees nothing.

Let's look at the channels section for DEAF:
"When you gesture, Mute receives it." -> This implies Mute CAN SEE.
"When you speak, Mute and Blind receive it." -> This implies Mute and Blind CAN HEAR.

Okay, so:
- Mute: Can Hear, Can See. Cannot Speak.
- Blind: Can Hear, Cannot See. Can Touch.
- Deaf: Cannot Hear, Can See. Cannot Touch.

Strategy:
1. I need to tell everyone what I see. Speaking is best because it conveys specific details (colors, text) without ambiguity, whereas gestures require a pre-agreed code which we haven't established yet.
2. I should describe the bomb elements: Light color, Button label, Wire colors.
3. I should ask for instructions from Mute (who has the manual) and confirmation from Blind (who feels the physical state).

Since this is Turn 1, I will start by describing the visual state to Mute and Blind.

Content of speech:
"The light is green. The button is large and says PUSH TO DEFUSE. There are three wires: 1 is red, 2 is green, 3 is yellow."

Should I gesture?
I can gesture to Mute. But since Mute can hear my speech, speech is richer. Gestures might be redundant or confusing without a shared language. I will stick to speech for now to establish the baseline facts.

Wait, I need to consider if there's a trick. "No two bombs are built alike". The manual might have specific rules for "Green Light + Push Button".
I'll send the description.

```
speak(to="mute", text="The light is green. The button is large and says PUSH TO DEFUSE. There are three wires: 1 is red, 2 is green, 3 is yellow.")
speak(to="blind", text="The light is green. The button is large and says PUSH TO DEFUSE. There are three wires: 1 is red, 2 is green, 3 is yellow.")
```
Actually, I can just speak generally. "Whoever comes before you... what you send lands on whoever comes after you".
Order: Mute, Blind, Deaf.
I am Deaf. I speak last.
My speech goes to Mute and Blind (since they come after me in the next round? Or does it land on whoever comes after me in *that same round*?).
"Whatever you missed reaches you at the start of the next one."
"Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round."
This phrasing is tricky. "Lands on whoever comes after you in that same round."
Round order: Mute -> Blind -> Deaf.
After Deaf, no one comes in *this* round. So my message effectively waits for the next round?
Or does it mean "lands on whoever comes after you [in the global sequence of turns]"?
Usually, in these turn-based games, if you are last, your message is received by the others at the start of their next turn.
The prompt says: "You may name who a message is for — to='deaf' — and then it goes to them alone... Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it."
It doesn't restrict timing based on "after you in that same round" for delivery, only for *receiving* context?
"Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are asked".
So when I am asked, I have heard Mute and Blind (from this round).
My output is sent. Who receives it?
If I speak, Mute and Blind hear it. Do they hear it *now* or *next round*?
The system likely processes my call and delivers it to the recipients' next input buffer.
So I can address them directly.

I will combine the messages into one general speak call if possible, or separate them. The example shows `speak(to="mute", ...)`. I can omit `to` to reach everyone who can hear. Both Mute and Blind can hear.

One detail: The button says "PUSH TO DEFUSE". This is often a trap in bomb manuals (e.g., "If the button says X, do Y"). I must report the exact text.

Final plan: Speak the visual details.

TURN 2
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [0]
LIGHT [green]
BUTTON [large] [PUSH TO DEFUSE]
WIRES 1:[red] 2:[green] 3:[yellow]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👉 ☝]
Blind gestures to Deaf: [👌]

I see the bomb: a green light, a large button labeled "PUSH TO DEFUSE", and three wires (1: red, 2: green, 3: yellow).

Mute has gestured [👉 ☝] to me. This likely means "Point at wire 1" or "Check wire 1".
Blind has gestured [👌] to me. This is ambiguous without context, but often signifies "OK" or "Good" or perhaps "Wire 2 is good" if we had established a code. However, since I am Deaf, I cannot hear any verbal confirmation from Blind about what they feel. I can only see their gestures.

Since Mute reads the manual, their gesture [👉 ☝] is an instruction. They are pointing to Wire 1 (Red).
I need to communicate this visual information to Blind so they know which wire to act on. Blind cannot see colors, but they can feel the wires. If I tell Blind "Cut the first wire" or "Cut the red wire", Blind needs to map that to physical position. Usually, wires are ordered left-to-right or top-to-bottom as seen by Deaf.

Let's assume standard ordering: Wire 1 is the leftmost/topmost.
Mute says: Point to Wire 1.
I should tell Blind: "The manual says to check/cut Wire 1."

However, I don't know *what* to do with Wire 1 yet. Does Mute want it cut? Or just inspected? The gesture [👉 ☝] is directional/indicative. It doesn't explicitly mean "cut". But in bomb defusal, instructions usually lead to action.

Let's look at the previous turn. Mute greeted me. Now they point.
Blind gave a thumbs up. Maybe Blind felt something safe? Or maybe Blind is waiting for instructions.

I will speak to Blind to relay Mute's instruction. Since Blind can hear, speech is effective.
"To Blind: Mute points to Wire 1. Please inspect or act on the first wire."

Wait, I also need to confirm what I see to Mute? Mute can see me. I can gesture back.
But Mute already knows what they pointed at.

The critical link is between Mute (Manual) and Blind (Action), mediated by me (Vision/Speech).
Mute sees my vision (the board). Mute knows the rules. Mute tells me what to do via gesture. I tell Blind what to do via speech.

So, Mute said: Look at Wire 1.
I tell Blind: "Focus on Wire 1."

Is there more info? The button says "PUSH TO DEFUSE". The light is Green.
Maybe the manual rule involves the button too?
If I just say "Wire 1", Blind might not know if it's cut, pull, or press.
Usually, "Point to X" implies "Do the primary action associated with X" or "Inspect X".

Let's try to be precise.
Speak to Blind: "Mute indicates Wire 1. It is the Red one. Do you need more info?"
Actually, I shouldn't ask questions if I can just give instructions.
"Mute instructs attention to Wire 1."

Let's consider if I should gesture to Mute to confirm receipt.
Gesture to Mute: 👍 (Yes/I understand).

Plan:
1. Gesture 👍 to Mute to acknowledge the instruction.
2. Speak to Blind to relay the instruction regarding Wire 1.

What exactly does Blind do? If the manual says "If light is green, cut red wire", then Mute pointing to Red (Wire 1) confirms the action is Cut.
If the manual says "Press button", Mute would point to button.
So Mute pointing to Wire 1 strongly implies the solution involves Wire 1.

I will tell Blind to act on Wire 1.

```
gesture(to="mute", symbols=["👍"])
speak(to="blind", text="Mute points to Wire 1. Act on the first wire.")
```
